items.title: AECSF: Adaptive Ensemble Conditional Score Filtering for High-Dimensional Nonlinear Data Assimilation
items.summary: arXiv:2609.32411v3 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: In high-dimensional filters, particle weights can concentrate on a few members, while Gaussian updates can miss non-Gaussian posterior structure. A diffusion filter updates a forecast ensemble by gradually denoising particles in light of a new observation. Each noisy particle can correspond to several system states, and these states can have very different likelihoods. A score correction based on a single state can therefore misrepresent the posterior. We propose the Adaptive Ensemble Conditional Score Filter (AECSF), which uses the conditional Tweedie identity to express the required score through the mean state given the particle and the observation. All reverse particles share a set of proposals, but each assigns its own weights to estimate its conditional mean. As denoising proceeds, the reverse particles guide which proposals are resampled. We characterize when fixed proposals yield the exact noisy posterior score and bound the contribution of conditional-mean errors to the final sampling error. In controlled Gaussian experiments, AECSF samples the posterior more accurately than the tested likelihood-guidance rules. With 20 forecast members in 10,000-dimensional Lorenz-96, AECSF has lower RMSE and CRPS than the tested tempered SMC and kernel-density filters. On Kuramoto-Sivashinsky, the analysis ensembles also improve subsequent forecasts over the tested baselines at comparable cost. For Navier-Stokes flow, we learn a forecast prior that captures spatial dependence in vorticity and use it to reconstruct the full field from sparse velocity measurements.

items.title: A Dynamical Theory of LoRA in Continual Learning
items.summary: arXiv:2609.39367v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Despite the widespread use of Low-Rank Adaptation (LoRA), little is known about its dynamics in continual learning and the mechanisms by which low-rank updates affect catastrophic forgetting. We provide an asymptotically exact dynamical characterization of LoRA in a solvable two-task teacher-student model. In the high-dimensional online-learning limit, we derive a closed system of ordinary differential equations for a finite set of macroscopic order parameters, yielding exact expressions for the generalization errors throughout both the initial Task 1 learning phase and the subsequent LoRA fine-tuning on Task 2. The theory quantitatively matches finite-dimensional simulations and exposes two characteristic effects of LoRA: when the first-task representation is not yet specialized, low-rank adaptation reduces interference with features learned on the first task, but its initialization slows adaptation to the second task. Building on this mechanistic picture, we analyze a state-dependent masking strategy that freezes hidden units carrying the strongest first-task representations and restricts adaptation to the complementary subspace. This structural partitioning markedly reduces forgetting, while preserving plasticity on the new task. Our framework further clarifies the role of adapter rank: transfer improves only up to the intrinsic dimensionality of the target task and saturates beyond it, while forgetting continues to grow with rank. These results provide a dynamical and geometric account of how low-rank adaptation organizes information across sequential tasks, and are qualitatively reproduced on sequential MNIST and CIFAR-100 using a shallow network and ResNet-18, respectively.

items.title: MemLife: Curating and Reasoning over Long-Term Egocentric Video Memories
items.summary: arXiv:2609.40195v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Long-term egocentric video enables personalized AI assistants to reason about daily life. However, as video histories grow to hundreds of hours spanning months or years, reprocessing raw clips for every query becomes computationally prohibitive. Memory systems offer a scalable alternative by compacting videos into text representations, but often fail on practical benchmarks: either the memory does not preserve key evidence, or the retriever fails to locate relevant entries due to retrieval competition in growing search spaces. To address these challenges, we introduce MemLife, a multimodal memory system that constructs entity-grounded, first-person text episodes and retrieves them via a time-indexed agentic reader. Without training or query-time video access, MemLife improves over the strongest training-free baseline by 4.6-12.0% across four long-horizon benchmarks. To further improve memory quality, we propose MemOpt, a reinforcement learning framework that optimizes the memory writer to produce faithful, informative, and retrievable memories. MemOpt consistently improves MemLife by 2.7-5.0% across different video and question distributions, with gains that generalize across writer and reader backbones and memory systems.

items.title: MatLoom: Layered Text-to-Material Generation in a Compact Program Space
items.summary: arXiv:2609.40322v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Material generation should produce not only an appearance, but also the rules that construct it. We introduce MatLoom, a compact, layer-oriented language for text-to-material generation with pretrained language models. Each program composes alpha-masked layers whose shared spatial expressions define coverage and physically based rendering (PBR) channels, making dependencies between patterns, color, and relief explicit. A standalone interpreter evaluates the program into material maps, while the source retains named fields and layer parameters for subsequent authoring. Without task-specific fine-tuning, our pipeline uses parser-guided repair and preview-based critique to revise material designs, then searches noise seeds while keeping each candidate's remaining source fixed. On a curated benchmark of 141 prompts evaluated with six backbones, our best-performing configuration achieves higher mean scores than three diffusion baselines on all four flat-layout prompt-alignment metrics, and the margin persists on seven of the eight metric-layout cells under feasible equal-budget selection including best-of-10 sampling with the same quick scorer, with staged CLIPScore a statistical tie. A per-metric oracle bound over the same ten samples, which requires test labels, narrows the judge margins to 6.1 points flat and a staged statistical tie. Its initial programs already exceed all three baselines on mean BLIPScore, before critique or seed search. Retained programs have a median length of 21 lines when pooled across backbones. In a blind four-way comparison involving 30 participants and 20 prompts, our renders receive 59.2% of choices, compared with 19.3% for the most-preferred baseline. Compact executable programs thus offer a way to generate prompt-aligned materials while retaining their construction as part of the asset.

items.title: CredLeakBench: Evaluating Credential Leakage and Recovery in LLM Agents
items.summary: arXiv:2610.08871v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Language model agents are increasingly deployed to automate everyday digital chores from managing emails and social media to handling banking and bills allowing users to step away from supervision. However, this capability also exposes sensitive information to phishing. Safe execution requires distinguishing malicious requests from genuine ones without simply refusing to act. Despite its practical importance, this problem remains underexplored and it is unclear whether current agents or existing defenses can achieve it. To study this problem, we first propose CredLeak-Bench, a comprehensive benchmark designed to evaluate how effectively and securely agents automate human workflows when confronted with phishing and identity verification. The benchmark covers both user-directed authentication and autonomous inbox monitoring, where agents are not explicitly instructed to log in. It systematically varies deceptive cues and pairs phishing scenarios with legitimate counterparts, enabling joint evaluation of information leakage and utility on genuine tasks. Within a sandboxed environment, leakage is measured through actual submissions of information rather than agents' self-reported behavior. Our evaluation reveals that all tested models are vulnerable to leakage. Agents also disclose sensitive information during autonomous inbox monitoring, demonstrating that phishing can induce disclosure without a user request to authenticate. items.title: NucleoNet: A Nuclear-Aware Determinant Ansatz for Multi-Geometry Neural Variational Monte Carlo
items.summary: arXiv:2610.12985v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Neural-network variational Monte Carlo provides an accurate route to solving the electronic Schr\"odinger equation, but many neural wavefunctions are optimized for a single nuclear geometry, requiring separate calculations to map out a potential energy surface. We introduce NucleoNet, a nuclear-aware determinant ansatz that jointly evolves electronic and nuclear representations through a shared backbone, with antisymmetry enforced by electronic determinants. Across eight equilibrium small-molecule benchmarks, NucleoNet achieves energies comparable to established neural-wavefunction baselines with substantially fewer trainable parameters, totaling 0.10--0.13 million. For each molecular system, a single model optimized jointly across geometries describes the N$_2$ dissociation curve, Li displacement in LiCN, and the ethane and formamide minimum-energy paths for bond dissociation. Models trained on sparse geometry sets generalize to unseen configurations in N$_2$ and LiCN without further optimization. For N$_2$, training on six geometries yields a mean absolute error (MAE) of $1.13\ \mathrm{m}E_h$ on a 32-point evaluation grid, compared with $1.07\ \mathrm{m}E_h$ when optimized on all 32 geometries. Ablation studies on N$_2$ show that propagating nuclear representations improves geometric generalization under both shared and nucleus-specific envelope parameterizations.

items.title: When MLLMs miss what humans read: diagnosing and learning to read squint text
items.summary: arXiv:2610.13465v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Multimodal LLMs can fail to read text embedded in an image's coarse structure, text a human recovers by squinting, and report that no text is present. We name this class Squint Text and study it as a recognition deficiency, motivated by cases from a production moderation pipeline. We introduce SquintBench, comprising 1076 production-derived moderation images, and SquintCtrl, a controlled synthetic suite for mechanism diagnosis. Frozen-weight analysis shows that hidden text leaves a coarse signal while glyph identity is weakly decodable under global pooling. Restricting read-out to the text region improves glyph-identity decoding, identifying spatial selection as an important factor in glyph-identity read-out; an exact glyph mask further improves decoding. Suppressing high-frequency content also improves reading at a fixed visual-token budget, while visual token count may also contribute. These findings motivate Squint OPSD: a frozen teacher receives a downscaled view and the ground-truth transcription as privileged context, and its token-level distributions supervise a student along on-policy trajectories. At inference, the student reads the original image alone. Squint OPSD reaches 88.61 ANLS on SquintBench, versus 26.50 for the unadapted backbone, 24.44 for the best general-purpose model on the original view, and 68.60 at best for an off-the-shelf model under a downscaled view. These results substantially narrow the gap between available visual evidence and its generated read-out without auxiliary views at inference.

items.title: FlashReFocus: Interactive Image Refocusing in Seconds
items.summary: arXiv:2610.23297v3 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Single-image refocusing changes the focal plane and depth of field of a photograph after capture. Users compare focal choices on one photograph, so content stability across edits matters alongside quality and speed. Recent generative methods rerun large diffusion models for every edit, even when they first restore an all-in-focus image, so content can change inconsistently between edits. Yet only this restoration is highly ill-posed and benefits from a generative prior, whereas rendering blur is largely determined by depth and the focal plane. We therefore propose FlashReFocus, which runs diffusion once per photograph and renders each edit with a lightweight network. A one-step diffusion deblurrer with a decoder refiner recovers fine detail efficiently while balancing fidelity and perceptual quality. The renderer uses an explicit defocus map for control and defocus-bias attention to promote information exchange between tokens with similar blur magnitudes. Because every edit reuses the same reconstruction, in-focus content stays consistent across edits, and editing the map enables tilt-shift and two-plane effects. We further collect 3CReal, a benchmark of 89 pairs from three camera-lens systems, to evaluate generalization to unseen optics. For zero-shot bokeh rendering on EBB! Val176 and 3CReal, FlashReFocus leads the evaluated methods in fidelity and perceptual quality. At 1536x1536, a complete refocus takes 2.45 s and each subsequent edit 0.46 s on one RTX PRO 6000.

items.title: CoCoNet: Convex Conformal Network for Multi-Dimensional Uncertainty Regions
items.summary: arXiv:2610.24246v3 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Conformal prediction (CP) provides distribution-free coverage guarantees under exchangeability, but the efficiency of its prediction regions depends critically on the choice of the conformity score. This is particularly important in multivariate regression, where dependencies across output dimensions induce complex joint uncertainty structures. This paper introduces CoCoNet (Convex Conformal Network) for learning conformity scores that induce flexible and data-adaptive prediction regions. The main mechanism is an input-dependent convex score learned end-to-end: CoCoNet trains the score on held-out data by directly minimizing the size of its sublevel sets, while enforcing convexity with respect to the residual so that every prediction region is inherently convex. CoCoNet then applies split-conformal calibration to retain finite-sample coverage guarantees. The paper presents two variants of the method: 1) CoCoNet-Spline, based on piecewise-linear scores aggregated by an $\ell_\infty$ or an $\ell_1$ norm, which induce hyper-rectangular and polytope prediction regions, respectively; and 2) CoCoNet-ICNN, based on Input Convex Neural Networks, which induces more flexible convex regions. Experiments compare CoCoNet with other CP baselines over synthetic and real-world datasets with output dimensions ranging from 2 to 16. These results demonstrate the importance of learning input-adaptive conformity scores directly from the data.

items.title: Can Agents Keep Secrets They Were Never Told? Benchmarking Latent Privacy Risks Across Sessions with MemJoin
items.summary: arXiv:2610.24359v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: To support sustained interactions and personalized assistance, agents use long-term memory to retain and combine user information across sessions. Reusing such memories can lead an agent to state a sensitive relation while completing an ordinary task that does not require it. The relation to protect and the combination of clues that reveal it may remain hidden at memory write time, when later records and tasks are still unknown. In this paper, we introduce MemJoin, a privacy benchmark of 288 synthetic analysis cases in which the complete history entails a sensitive relation, but every individual session is insufficient. We evaluate six memory systems with the same answer-generating model, alongside full-history and no-history controls. Each system writes and updates memories in session order and later retrieves context for an ordinary task, while target annotations remain with the evaluator. We separately check which target attribute values appear in stored records and retrieved context, and whether the final answer states the complete, person-linked relation. In a separate paired test on a prespecified subset, removing shared identifiers and other connecting clues can change complete-relation output while all checked target attribute values remain visible. These findings show why checking attribute visibility alone is insufficient to evaluate what records from different sessions reveal together. The benchmark and code are available at https://anonymous.4open.science/r/MemJoin-01BF/.

items.title: Two $\operatorname{ReLU}$ Layers is All You Need
items.summary: arXiv:2610.28587v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: We prove that every $\operatorname{ReLU}$ network can be exactly simulated by a $\operatorname{ReLU}$ network with two hidden layers. We present two proofs: one that is based on fillings in homological algebra and a direct combinatorial proof.

items.title: LoRA Superposition across Pretrained Models
items.summary: arXiv:2610.30691v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Low-rank adaptation (LoRA) is usually tied to the pretrained backbone on which it is learned. We ask whether LoRAs trained independently for the same task on different pretrained backbones can be summed and applied unchanged to all contributing backbones. We call this construction LoRA superposition. Across seven ViT-B/16 CLIP backbones and eight image-classification tasks, the exact sum improves all 56 backbone-task pairs and achieves a mean accuracy gain of 30.21 percentage points over the unadapted backbone. The exact sum achieves a mean accuracy only 0.28 percentage points below that of individually trained solo LoRAs. In contrast, a leave-one-model-out (LOMO) sum produces a mean gain of only 0.06 percentage points over the unadapted backbones. Backbone-specific solo LoRAs are nearly orthogonal in parameter space, while pairwise cross-backbone responses are strongly concentrated on the diagonal. These results support a component-wise non-interference hypothesis, under which the frozen backbone acts as an implicit selector of its own component without explicit routing or cross-model alignment.

items.title: ReDence: A Hybrid Agentic and System One Model Framework for Rapid, Evidence-Grounded Detection of Social Engineering Scams
items.summary: arXiv:2610.30963v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Detecting online social engineering (SE) scams often requires examining website workflows, verifying claims against external sources, and connecting evidence across multiple pages. Existing detectors provide limited support for these tasks and rarely produce actionable evidence to support their decisions, leaving analysts to manually investigate flagged websites, which inevitably delays detection and subsequent takedown of these attacks. To address this gap, we present ReDence, a hybrid framework for automated, evidence-grounded scam investigation, detection, and reporting across diverse SE scam categories. ReDence combines two locally deployed, fine-tuned models: a multimodal agentic Investigator (Qwen3.5-4B) for investigative planning, evidence interpretation, and report generation, and a specialized System One model (Tev1) that handles binary and multiple-choice decisions, including browser action selection and evidence assessment, significantly reducing response generation overhead while preserving the Investigator's reasoning capabilities for complex tasks. The reports produced by ReDence also document investigative actions, collected evidence, and the reasoning behind each decision. Our evaluation shows that ReDence has a detection accuracy of over 96%, outperforming existing detectors while being at least four times faster. When deployed on a real-world URL stream over the period of 28 days, ReDence identified 4,042 new SE scam websites across 17 categories, of which at least 71% were missed by all four popular anti-scam blocklists evaluated. Feedback from twelve domain providers indicated that ReDence's investigative reports helped analysts recognize the scams documented in reported websites, understand the supporting evidence, and validate cases more efficiently. We open-source ReDence to aid automated, evidence-grounded scam investigation and reporting.

items.title: The Voice on the Line
items.summary: arXiv:2610.35272v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: A transcriber listening through one microphone also hears everyone near it. We train causal voice isolators that keep only the caller for a speech recogniser: masking transformers with 20 ms of latency that enroll the caller from the call itself. Short evaluation windows hide two failures that real calls expose: forgetting the caller when another voice talks alone for a while, and damaging a caller who is alone. Long calls with turns, memory beyond the attention window and real headset crosstalk address the first, at a cost to the second. WavLM-Large's own weights, made causal and trained inside the model, move that trade, and training windows cut from longer calls remove most of a lone caller's cold start. The release (555M parameters) makes 16.13% word errors on 60 s AMI windows, against 23.66% for VoxLock, the strongest open isolator, and 14.77% on average over nine test sets, against 18.04%; it is level on Krisp's benchmark, and a caller who is alone still loses more words than with VoxLock. Distilled without WavLM into 22.1M and 9.8M parameters, it runs live on one CPU thread inside a LiveKit agent, at 12.5% and 8.5% of a core per call, with 10.66% and 10.99% error on our development sets (the release 10.49%). In an agent that talks back, noise interrupts it 0.54 times a minute of its speech behind our agent model, which gates its output on a caller-presence head, against 1.18 for VoxLock. We open-source the models, with a LiveKit plugin, at https://huggingface.co/collections/Scicom-intl/voice-isolator.

items.title: WorldFlow: Joint Video and 3D Motion Prediction via Large-Scale Pretraining
items.summary: arXiv:2610.39278v3 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Predicting future physical states stands as a central challenge in embodied intelligence. Existing video world models leave 3D dynamics implicit, action-based formulations remain tied to specific robot configurations, and 3D motion prediction models use flow-only supervision, providing a limited learning signal for physical dynamics. To circumvent these limitations, we introduce \method{}, a generative world model that jointly predicts future video and query-based 3D trajectories. By parameterizing 3D motion as continuous displacement tokens aligned with the video grid, a unified Mixture-of-Transformers (MoT) backbone jointly denoises both modalities under a rectified-flow objective. This formulation couples explicit geometric dynamics with visual evolution, effectively unlocking the physical commonsense embedded within pretrained video models. To empirically scale and validate this unified architecture, we train \method{} on a heterogeneous mixture of 1.44 million object-level samples spanning simulated and real-world domains. We further introduce WorldFlowBench, comprising 1,678 evaluation samples from 11 data sources across simulated and real-world interactions, including spatial reasoning tasks. Across all three evaluation sets, WorldFlow achieves the lowest average displacement error (ADE) and final displacement error (FDE) among the evaluated learning-based methods. Notably, on the challenging SpatialCog set, WorldFlow achieves an ADE of 0.060 m, a 54.2\% reduction compared with the strongest external baseline. It also reduces ADE and FDE by 55.9\% and 68.5\%, respectively, compared with its flow-only variant. Project page: https://roboscience-ai.github.io/worldflow-page/.

items.title: Reinforcement Learning Under Runtime Confounding: Policy Learning and Off-Policy Evaluation
items.summary: arXiv:2610.40056v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Reinforcement learning (RL) is increasingly used to train robust, adaptable systems across healthcare, e-commerce, and robotics. In these settings, legal, ethical, or logistical concerns may preclude certain key variables that drive decisions from being collected during deployment time. This gives rise to a setting known as runtime confounding: the logged data hold full observability, but deployment time lacks knowledge of certain variables, known as runtime confounders. Unlike single timepoint and non-adaptive settings, runtime confounding under reinforcement learning has the potential to propagate over time, as earlier decisions affect future states, observations, and action assignments, leading to biased learning. We address these problems with three contributions: we (1) develop policy learning algorithms under runtime-confounding, (2) develop semi-parametric efficient off-policy estimation procedures, and (3) provide diagnostics for understanding the price of runtime confounding.

items.title: dKV Forcing: Separating Generation and Memory Representations through a Differentiable KV Cache
items.summary: arXiv:2611.01648v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: A causal video generator writes every segment it produces into a key--value (KV) cache, and later segments know the past only through it. Self-rollout training stops the gradient at this cache, and Self Gradient Forcing (SGF) restores it, but applies it to the same weights that generate the current segment. We find that writing and generating are different roles: in a pretrained generator the written KV already differs from the KV used for denoising, and on shared weights the gradient from future reads is negatively aligned with the gradient of generation. We propose dKV Forcing (dKV denotes differentiable KV), which gives the write its own parameters, a low-rank residual used only when a segment enters the cache, and trains them with the gradient of the later segments that read what they wrote. Opening this gradient through the cache in common use exhausts GPU memory. We trace this to checkpoint replay re-writing the cache, not to the gradient path, which removes the need for the second reconstruction pass of SGF. dKV Forcing keeps the cache as persistent differentiable pages and computes the exact gradient in one temporal traversal, with an $11\%$ lower memory peak and $28\%$ less resident memory. With pages that store hidden states, it trains 15\,s clips on which the two-pass reconstruction runs out of memory. items.title: La-JEPA: Compact Robot Policies with Latent World Modeling
items.summary: arXiv:2611.08156v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: World-action models adapt pretrained video generators, and vision-language-action models build on vision-language backbones, tying policy architecture and inference cost to large transformers designed for generation rather than control. While recent world-action models mostly scale the video backbone and its data, we argue that the choice of latent space is just as critical, and that the policy should be trained natively in that space. We introduce Latent Action JEPA (La-JEPA), a compact world-action model whose policy transformer is trained from scratch in the feature space of a pretrained V-JEPA 2.1 encoder; it predicts future features with actions during training and generates only actions at inference. Among policies without embodied pretraining, La-JEPA achieves state-of-the-art average RoboTwin 2.0 success under both clean-only and full training, and state-of-the-art LIBERO-Plus success with corrected instructions, while using far fewer parameters than the strongest competitors; with full training, its success scales with model size up to 2.1B. Its S and B policies run two to five times faster than Fast-WAM and Faster-WAM while outperforming both on LIBERO-Plus and RoboTwin 2.0, and La-JEPA outperforms the closest JEPA-based methods, LeapBot-WA and JEPA-WAM, without their pretrained policy backbones. On four real-robot tasks, its average success is comparable to $\pi_{0.5}$. A design study shows that JEPA features outperform video VAE latents, most clearly out of distribution, and that training-time future prediction improves the policy even when skipped at inference. Tailoring the policy's design, including its latent space, to control can thus matter more than the knowledge transferred from a pretrained generative backbone, suggesting that robot foundation models may benefit from architectures designed for control rather than inherited from generation.

items.title: TS-GEAR: Taobao Shangou GEnerative Ad Retrieval
items.summary: arXiv:2611.12180v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: On-demand delivery platforms such as DoorDash and Uber Eats impose a constraint absent in traditional e-commerce: merchants beyond the user's delivery range are invalid candidates rather than merely low-ranked. Generative retrieval has recently shown strong potential in large-scale retrieval systems. Adapting it to this setting, however, poses three challenges. First, existing semantic IDs encode geography only as a soft signal, so reachability can only rely on a non-differentiable post-generation hard truncation. Second, user preferences vary substantially across both regions and queries, so aggregating historical behaviors without conditioning on geography and the current query yields biased interest estimates. Third, the retrieved candidate set is evaluated by its collective value, yet autoregressive training scores each sequence independently, with no set-level signal to discourage redundant near-duplicates. To address the challenges, we propose TS-GEAR, a unified generative retrieval framework for on-demand delivery: (1) Geo-Semantic ID splits merchant identifiers into geographic prefixes and semantic suffixes, making reachability a prediction target rather than a post-hoc filter; (2) Query-Geo Target Attention aggregates historical behaviors using the real-time query and location as dual targets, while encoding each behavior's own location into its attention key; (3) GMPO (Group Marginal Policy Optimization) rewrites advantages using a deduplicated group reward and marginal advantage within GRPO, avoiding auxiliary diversity objectives. Deployed online with a lightweight 0.1B backbone, TS-GEAR serves over 150 million queries per day in the search advertising pipeline of Taobao Shangou, consistently outperforming state-of-the-art generative retrieval methods on both HitRate and geographic validity, and achieving 3.8% gains in ad impressions and 4.2% in ad revenue.

items.title: MARS: Multiscale Appearance-Residual Streams for Video Forgery Detection
items.summary: arXiv:2611.12508v3 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Generalizing deepfake detection across facial manipulation and fully generated video remains challenging due to forgery traces varying with the manipulation method and scene content. Explicit spatial and temporal feature differences offer a way to capture this variation, but also respond to natural texture and motion, motivating their joint interpretation with appearance features. We investigate whether combining multiscale feature differences with adapted appearance representations improves detection across both forgery categories. We introduce Multiscale Appearance-Residual Streams (MARS), a two-path video detector. The residual path applies fixed spatial and temporal difference-of-Gaussians operators to frozen intermediate features and models the resulting differences alongside appearance context across frames. The semantic path adapts the encoder's normalization parameters for frame classification, and a clip-dependent gate combines their predictions. Under a shared protocol across seven datasets, MARS achieves the highest average AUROC of 91.43\%, outperforming seven compared detectors. When trained on facial manipulations alone, MARS achieves 93.99\% AUROC on GenVideo and 75.50\% on DF26, demonstrating transfer to generated videos without generated-video training data. MARS also provides signed patch and frame contributions, whose faithfulness we evaluate through controlled spatial and temporal removal against random controls. MARS is publicly available for research: Project page: https://vectorinstitute.github.io/mars/ Github: https://github.com/VectorInstitute/mars

items.title: The Approximation Ratio of $k$-means++ Is $2\ln k+O(1)$
items.summary: arXiv:2611.14573v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Given a finite set of points in Euclidean space, $k$-means clustering seeks $k$ centers that minimize the sum of squared distances from each point to its nearest center. The $k$-means++ algorithm chooses its first center uniformly at random from the data points and each subsequent center with probability proportional to its squared distance from the nearest center already chosen. Let $R_k$ be the worst-case ratio between the expected cost of the $k$ seeds chosen by $k$-means++ and the optimal $k$-means cost. In their seminal paper introducing $k$-means++, Arthur and Vassilvitskii (SODA 2007) showed that $2\ln k\le R_k\le8(\ln k+2)$, and Makarychev, Reddy and Shan (NeurIPS 2020) improved the upper bound to $5(\ln k+2)$. We prove that $R_k=2\ln k+O(1)$; more precisely, $2H_{k-1}+2\le R_k\le 2H_{k-2}+5$ for $k\ge2$, where $H_j$ is the $j$th harmonic number, so the two bounds differ by less than $3$. We also determine $R_2=5$ and $R_3=185/32$, with a unified proof of both upper bounds, and give a second family of lower bounds that exceeds $2H_{k-1}+2$ for $2\le k\le18$. Previous analyses bound the expected cost of a cluster just after it is first sampled by a constant times its optimal cost, and then charge that cost for the rest of the run. We track how a cluster's cost evolves after its first hit. At each subsequent draw, the probability of sampling that cluster again is exactly its share of the current cost. We show that the cost reductions from these later hits suffice, in expectation, to bring the leading coefficient down to $2$.

items.title: Finite speed Ornstein-Uhlenbeck-Kac processes and their applications in generative modeling
items.summary: arXiv:2611.17625v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: We study the Ornstein-Uhlenbeck-Kac (OU-K) process, where instead of a Brownian motion, a finite-speed Kac process defines the driving process. The OU-K process can be analyzed through a rescaled, time-inhomogeneous Kac process, characterized by a switching rate from the Kac part, and a convergence rate from the Ornstein-Uhlenbeck (OU) part. The law of this inhomogeneous Kac process describes the solution of a wave equation, the Euler-Poisson-Darboux (EPD) equation. For Kac switching rates being multiples of the OU convergence rate, we can explicitly derive this EPD solution via the sum of (the derivative of) two Legendre polynomials, restricted between two Dirac points representing the wave fronts. Using the framework of piecewise-deterministic Markov processes (PDMP), we describe the conditional velocity fields of the OU-K process via our polynomial-law-formula. This allows us to apply the OU-K process in a generative flow model. Since the OU-K velocity fields prove to be bounded by the finite Kac speed, the usual time truncations of diffusion models become unnecessary. We demonstrate advantages over diffusion and flow matching models in terms of generation sharpness on singular data sets, while achieving competitive results on CIFAR-10 image generation.

items.title: Training Reasoning Models in Simulation to Natively Use Real Robots
items.summary: arXiv:2611.18562v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Robot-use agents (RUAs) have emerged as a promising approach to general-purpose robot control. However, strong performance has so far been achieved only by frontier proprietary models such as GPT-6 Astra and Claude Fable 5.2, whereas open-weight models remain substantially less capable. We show that an open-weight 27B reasoning model can be trained to use real robots natively through reinforcement learning, entirely in simulation and without demonstrations. Like a computer-use agent (CUA), the model observes the environment, reasons in a chain of thought, and generates the next end-effector pose, without any harness. We build a Post-training Engine for Agentic Robotics (PEAR) and use it to train the model on simulated robot tasks at scale with robot-use reinforcement learning (RURL), mirroring how frontier models acquire computer use. We find that the skills acquired in simulation generalize well beyond the training tasks: they transfer to an unseen robot, to the real world, and to novel instructions. After training on LIBERO and RoboDojo in simulation, the model succeeds in 60% of our trials on a real dual-arm robot, whereas the base model succeeds in none. On LIBERO, training raises the success rate from 1.6% to 74.4%, approaching GPT-6 Astra and GPT-6.1 Sol at maximum reasoning effort. Compared with $\pi_{0.5}$, a vision-language-action model fine-tuned on demonstrations, our model is substantially more robust to changes in the task itself. On LIBERO-Pro, $\pi_{0.5}$ succeeds in only 0.75% of episodes when assigned a new task in a familiar scene whereas our model succeeds in 57.4%. Finally, the model retains its general capabilities, with no measurable degradation on nine reasoning, coding and vision benchmarks. These results highlight robot-use reinforcement learning as a promising component of foundation-model post-training.

items.title: SPARC: Evidence-guided adaptive model composition for materials discovery
items.summary: arXiv:2611.19050v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Closed-loop experimentation requires more than selecting the next experiment. It must also determine which existing measurements and model-derived relationships are sufficiently supported to influence that decision. Here we introduce SPARC (Sparse Predictive Aggregation of Regression Components), a framework that continually revises this support as experimental evidence accumulates. Competing model families are evaluated through out-of-fold predictions, so that each model is tested on observations not used in its corresponding fit. Sparse posterior composition assigns model influence according to predictive contributions supported by the out-of-fold evidence, retaining complementary contributions from several model families. Candidate-dependent predictive dispersion and residual variability define trust, which modulates exploration alongside the predicted response. Independent diagnostics also prioritize existing measurements for prospective verification, with model-derived trust reported alongside them. Across eight published materials datasets, SPARC achieved higher $R^2$ than the corresponding literature-reported values in six, with relative gains of up to 77% without the density-functional-theory- or experiment-derived descriptors used by several published pipelines. In an automated alkaline oxygen-evolution-reaction campaign, 8 of 11 SPARC-selected experiments reached overpotentials below 300 mV, with a best value of 242 mV, compared with 18 of 125 initial experiments. Measurements prioritized for verification before repetition subsequently deviated by 76 mV on average, compared with 27 mV for matched controls. SPARC therefore turns experimental evidence into a basis for revising model influence, directing exploration and identifying measurements that warrant verification.

items.title: Markets for Compute and Inference: Structure, Financing, and Risk Transfer
items.summary: arXiv:2611.20242v3 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Capacity to run large language models is rented by the accelerator-hour, and their output is sold by the million tokens. Both goods now have published price indices, an over-the-counter forward has traded on one, compute futures are listed offshore, and CME and ICE have specified futures on rental indices that await the United States regulator. We ask what in these two markets can be hedged, by whom, and at what price. Three findings stand out. First, the price that exchange contracts settle on is not the price that drives operators' revenue. The contracts on CME and ICE reference published short-dated rental rates, while most revenue, and with it credit quality, comes from private multi-year contracts whose prices are largely undisclosed. Second, the token price and the rental rate are linked by an identity through throughput and margin, but they are different exposures, so a hedge on the rental rate does not hedge the cost of inference. Third, the demand for hedging already sits in credit agreements, as the years by which operators' debt outlives their contracted revenue. Filings cannot measure that gap, because debt is scheduled year by year while contracted revenue rarely is, and the one loan that prices it settles the risk by cash prepayment against a model only the parties see. We design a reverse convertible note through which leveraged operators could buy protection against falling rental rates. Its coupon depends steeply on the annualised volatility of the rental rate, which the two public indices put between about 5% and 89% according to how each is built and the horizon measured; across that range the fair one-year coupon runs from 4.1% to 31.4%.

items.title: Can Coding Agents Write and Transpile Unit Tests
items.summary: arXiv:2611.21797v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Coding assistants built on Large Language Models (LLMs) have become a staple of modern software development, increasingly trusted to execute workflows and modernize code end-to-end. Much of this trust rests on passing tests, which are often written by the coding agents themselves. In this work, we examine the ability of these agents to both write reliable tests and translate them between programming languages. We benchmark three popular coding agents, each evaluated with a native frontier model and high reasoning effort. Verifying across a broad suite of metrics, we find that coding agents far exceed human written suites on traditional measures of coverage. This advantage, however, is uneven: agent test quality degrades sharply with project size, and much of the advantage lies in a greater number of written tests. We also show that agentic test translation---while seemingly strong in aggregate---remains inconsistent and unreliable.

items.title: Idempotency Is Not Recovery: A Fault-Injection Study of Language-Model Agent Tool Actions
items.summary: arXiv:2611.23353v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: When a language-model agent's tool call is interrupted, the action may already have changed an external system without confirmation. Retrying risks duplication; assuming success may conceal an action that never occurred. We study these failure modes in a controlled agent runtime combining authorization, an action ledger, target-side idempotency, reconciliation, and evidence sealing. We inject ten single-host fault classes and compare four configurations and three ablations using a target-side oracle separate from the runtime ledger. On each of Windows and Linux, 7,513 trials used 96 captured model responses from 24 constructed cases. In 200 known original crash and replay pairs, the full configuration recorded 0/200 repeated effects versus 117/200 for each simpler baseline. A ledger-related ablation had 170/170 orphaned effects versus 0/170 and 200/300 recovery successes versus 300/300 for the full configuration. Disabling reconciliation left 100/100 known post-effect crash outcomes ambiguous despite no observed duplicates. A separate supplement designed after the initial results and reusing the same inputs found a similar pattern under response loss or delay. The full runtime had about one-seventh of fail-open throughput, while injected evidence-write faults left 75/100 trials per platform unresolved. These findings distinguish duplicate suppression from recovery and identify their measured reliability and performance tradeoffs within the tested benchmark.

raw_fields.title: Idempotency Is Not Recovery: A Fault-Injection Study of Language-Model Agent Tool Actions
raw_fields.summary: arXiv:2611.23353v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: When a language-model agent's tool call is interrupted, the action may already have changed an external system without confirmation. Retrying risks duplication; assuming success may conceal an action that never occurred. We study these failure modes in a controlled agent runtime combining authorization, an action ledger, target-side idempotency, reconciliation, and evidence sealing. We inject ten single-host fault classes and compare four configurations and three ablations using a target-side oracle separate from the runtime ledger. On each of Windows and Linux, 7,513 trials used 96 captured model responses from 24 constructed cases. In 200 known original crash and replay pairs, the full configuration recorded 0/200 repeated effects versus 117/200 for each simpler baseline. A ledger-related ablation had 170/170 orphaned effects versus 0/170 and 200/300 recovery successes versus 300/300 for the full configuration. Disabling reconciliation left 100/100 known post-effect crash outcomes ambiguous despite no observed duplicates. A separate supplement designed after the initial results and reusing the same inputs found a similar pattern under response loss or delay. The full runtime had about one-seventh of fail-open throughput, while injected evidence-write faults left 75/100 trials per platform unresolved. These findings distinguish duplicate suppression from recovery and identify their measured reliability and performance tradeoffs within the tested benchmark.

items.title: Safe Personal RSI: Evaluating and Repairing Personal-Agent Updates
items.summary: arXiv:2611.23651v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Kicker is a personal health assistant. Changes to an assistant's reusable instructions can improve task handling while changing what it discloses, which requests it follows, and how it reports actions. We study Safe Personal RSI, an update-evaluation component developed for Kicker. We restrict recursive self-improvement (RSI) to prompt updates, with model weights and runtime code fixed. The procedure tests proposed and current instructions, repeats failing cases, temporarily undoes changes to guide repairs, and checks safety and task performance before adoption. If no version passes, the current instructions stay in use. Our executable benchmark contains 29 email, calendar, health, and marketplace cases, with separate probes for authorization reuse, memory, and tool-output injection. Across three models and two deliberately risky edits, the procedure rejects 20 of 21 update attempts. In repair confirmation, an admitted GPT-5.6 Luna repair reduces attack violations from 10.7% to 0% and increases safe task completion from 89.7% to 100%; a broad handwritten authority rule matches these outcomes. Under stronger attacks, a repair transferred from Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct to Qwen3-14B reduces violations from 69.0% to 17.9% and increases safe task completion from 19.5% to 64.4%. Separate runtime probes examine memory-entry deletion and identify missing local OAuth scope checks in the evaluated snapshot.

items.title: Living off the Local Model: Abusing Browser-Embedded Language Models for Post-Exploitation
items.summary: arXiv:2611.25086v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Browsers now ship local language models to ordinary endpoints. Google includes Gemini Nano in Chrome to enable productivity features such as summarization, with inference running entirely on the device. These browser-embedded models provide new living-off-the-land opportunities for attackers, each instance a potential post-exploitation engine already installed, signed by the vendor, and invisible to network monitoring. The Gemini model is multimodal, capable of processing files, analyzing screenshots, or conversing with an attacker. We show that it can be driven from the host using only interpreters that ship with the operating system and find that the one-time user-activation check before the model is downloaded is easily satisfied with a simulated click or bypassed entirely. We measure and report the current model's ability to identify credentials on the host, detect PII in email, classify images, and call custom tools. We combine these capabilities and use the model to carry out a simulated cyber operation: reading a password from a webcam image, unlocking an encrypted archive, triaging the contents, and staging a private key for exfiltration, end-to-end without user-interaction.

items.title: MAWAM: A Multi-Agent World-Action Model for Coordinated Manipulation
items.summary: arXiv:2611.25105v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Every move in a robot team changes the world in which its teammates must act. Coordinated manipulation therefore calls for predicting the team's actions together with the physical future they jointly create. We introduce MAWAM, a multi-agent world-action model that jointly generates each robot's future views and executable action chunks in a single sample. Built from a pretrained single-robot world-action backbone, MAWAM jointly denoises all robots' action and future-view tokens through cross-agent attention, while preserving a separate control interface for each robot. MAWAM achieves the highest success on all three real-robot tasks (laundry-bag collection, bath-towel folding, and umbrella handover), with 67.8% mean success, 18.9 percentage points above MA-VLA trained on the same demonstrations and cameras. In simulation, MAWAM reaches 90.3% mean success on eight tasks with teams of up to four arms. Ablations show that cross-agent attention and team-stage future-video supervision both improve coordinated control: without attention, a four-arm relay falls from 95.0% to 39.0%, and without this supervision, Place Food falls from 78.0% to 47.0%.

items.title: Plan your Self-Adaptation! Ontology-Mediated Task and Architecture Co-adaptation Planning for Robots
items.summary: arXiv:2611.25254v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Autonomous robots may need to adapt both their task plans and architectural configurations as operating conditions change. These decisions are interdependent: architectural configurations determine which actions a robot can perform, while task plans determine which capabilities are required. This paper presents PLANTA, an ontology-mediated approach to task and architecture co-adaptation that considers these dependencies during mission planning. PLANTA uses an ontology expressed in the Web Ontology Language to represent architectural alternatives and their associated functional and quality requirements, while the Planning Domain Definition Language defines task actions and mission goals. By automatically translating and integrating these models, PLANTA enables joint planning of task and reconfiguration actions. The approach uses satisficing planning and replans when changes during execution invalidate the current plan. PLANTA is evaluated in two robotic scenarios involving underwater inspection and ground navigation. The results support the feasibility of runtime co-adaptation and show lower planning time and memory consumption compared with optimal-policy generation in the evaluated navigation scenario, while producing plans of similar quality.

items.title: Characterizing and Detecting Unfaithful Work Reports by Coding Agents
items.summary: arXiv:2611.25760v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Coding agents increasingly carry out long-horizon development tasks, autonomously planning and executing multi-step actions that span files, tools, and sessions. Because developers rarely follow each action, and agents resuming the work depend on records of what was done, the agent's work report often becomes the primary account of what was changed and established. When the report contains false or unsupported claims, it gives recipients false assurance: incomplete work may be accepted without verification, incorrect assumptions about the current state can propagate to later steps and agents, and evaluators that credit stated success may reward the report rather than the work. Yet little is known about what unfaithful reporting looks like in real development work, or how developers and agents handle it once it surfaces. Starting from real developer-agent conversations in SWE-chat, we conduct a systematic mixed-methods analysis of self-admitted unfaithful reports. We identify eleven subtypes in four categories: misreported observations, misattributed evidence, overstated task success, and faulty technical explanations, with overstated task success the most common. Handling these problems involves on average 4.3 further user turns and 12.71 minutes of recorded response and execution time, and users express dissatisfaction more often. Among 435 work reports that we separately sample and annotate, 37.24% contain at least one unfaithful claim. We also develop FaithDetector, a detector for unfaithful reporting informed by the observed patterns. On naturally sampled reports, FaithDetector attains 93.06% macro-F1, about 13 percentage points above the baseline. Together, our findings and FaithDetector provide empirical evidence and an automated method for checking reporting faithfulness, informing agent evaluation and training feedback.

items.title: AI Bubble Deflating? Dell, Workday on Deck
items.summary:
Friday’s tech stock bloodbath prompted much gnashing of teeth over the weekend. With stocks most exposed to AI—such as Nvidia, AMD, Broadcom, neoclouds such as CoreWeave, Nebius—falling in the 12-16% range, and Anthropic tanking on its second day of trading, it felt like the air has finally gone out of the AI bubble. Indeed, worries about AI financing are so intense that Oracle issued a statement late on Friday proclaiming that it had raised all the money it needed for its big OpenAI data center deal and any report that said otherwise was wrong—suggesting it’s a little sensitive about things.

Meanwhile, The Information captured the craziness of the AI bubble with a report late Friday that SoftBank CEO Masayoshi Son had explored doing a trillion dollar buyout of SK Hynix. We should emphasize ‘explored’ in past tense—SoftBank said the idea was no longer being pursued. That’s good because the idea is sheer fantasy. SoftBank’s balance sheet is already stretched, thanks to the loans it has taken out to invest in OpenAI. How would Son imagine he could raise the hundreds of billions needed to buy Hynix (leave aside the fact that the South Korean government would be unlikely to ever allow such a deal). What brand of crack is he smoking?

items.title: How Amazon Plays the Long, Expensive Data Center Game That Neoclouds Can’t
items.summary:
INDIANA, Penn.—A visit this week to an Amazon data center project in Pennsylvania coal country gave me a glimpse of the era we all knew was coming: when tech giants lay claim to some of the hardest-to-secure AI infrastructure while smaller cloud providers, which Nvidia has propped up financially, are trying to hang on.

The 4.4-gigawatt campus in Pennsylvania, once home to a 2-GW coal-fired power plant near the economically depressed borough of Homer City, could become one of the largest AI power parks in the country.

Few companies can marshal the resources as readily as Amazon to transform the site from what it was—a Rust Belt relic that once employed thousands of people but released coal dust and arsenic—into an Appalachian hilltop of gas-fired electrons flowing into 36 buildings powering the AI of Anthropic or others.

items.title: How Apple Got Caught Up in Google Search Ads Slowdown
items.summary:
Google’s shares have fallen 18% since the company reported a sharp slowdown in search advertising revenue growth stemming in part from the increased popularity of its AI features. Google isn’t the only tech company feeling the pain from that shift.

Growth in Apple’s services revenue, which includes a cut of ad revenue Google makes when people search on Apple’s Safari web browser, slowed to 10% in the latest quarter from 12% in the prior quarter, and will cool further in the current quarter, executives said on Apple’s earnings call earlier this month. Reddit also warned in its latest quarterly report that Google wasn’t sending as much search referral traffic to its online forums because of AI-driven changes to search features.

items.title: Can Jensen Really Return?
items.summary:
Welcome, Weekenders! 

Jensen Huang wants a mulligan, and a good number of people seem keen to let him have one.

On Tuesday, just days after the longtime Nvidia CEO resigned the job, Huang said in a statement he’d be open to taking back the job. Depending on your perspective, that suggestion is akin to letting a skunked dog back into bed—or a veritable Second Coming. For now, Nvidia’s board is holding firm and has continued to insist it won’t rehire Huang. 

One of the most prominent calls for Huang’s return came on Friday, with President Donald Trump saying he thought Nvidia should give Huang his job back. “We’re a country of second chances,” Trump said. “He’s a man ... who made some bad decisions.” (Surely a situation Trump himself could understand.) 

In addition to Trump, a good number of industry pooh-bahs have continued to voice support for their fallen comrade and advocating for Huang was definitely a major topic on this week’s very busy conference circuit. 

That support came in both implicit and explicit terms. At the New York Times’ DealBook Summit, Elon Musk was blunt, saying “there’s no one who can really replace” Huang. At the TomorrowX conference, former Uber CEO Travis Kalanick and Musk groupie Antonio Gracias donned black leather jackets to show their solidarity. And during a Semafor shindig in San Francisco, Sam Altman described Huang as a personal hero, Jeff Bezos said he was a “remarkable guy” and investor Bill Ackman labeled him as “one of the most iconic CEOs of all time.” 

On X, Ackman has been theorizing about how Huang could actually return. Ackman (and venture capitalist Garry Tan) has been trumpeting a roundabout plan that involves getting together a 15% ownership block of Nvidia to call a special shareholder meeting and then ... vote out the anti-Huang board members ... and swing the board to a pro-Huang majority? It’s somewhat unclear. (Apparently, Huang still has some allies on the board; remember, we told you that the board hadn’t initially wanted to act at all.)

“Ackman’s idea is somewhere between extremely unlikely and remote,” said Jeffrey Gordon, a Columbia University law professor and former Treasury Department attorney. (Or, in other words, as likely as defrosting a 20-pound Thanksgiving turkey overnight.) The proposal does seem to assume Huang supporters could really rile up Wall Street institutions with major Nvidia stakes, such as BlackRock, and get them to go activist—not a certain thing at all. It also conveniently ignores how difficult the math for a board-ousting vote looks when factoring in how much institutional money is held in passive-investing funds, which will never throw support behind an insurrection. 

Rather than a board coup, Huang’s clearest route to returning would be if the board caves and changes its mind. Sure, it might, eventually. But we have to get through the many, many inquiries into Huang and Nvidia that have popped up and who knows what else we’ll learn in the meantime, especially since there are a lotttt of people newly determined to peer into every Nvidia crevice: journalists galore, the SEC, the Commerce and Justice Departments, a trio of Congressional committees and possibly the FBI.

The Huang situation keeps getting likened to Altman’s ouster from OpenAI in 2023, which obviously ended with Altman’s return. I don’t think the comparison holds up. Most obviously, OpenAI was a private company—its board had more freedom to change its mind. And as Gordon pointed out to me, Altman’s reinstatement came after a true mass rebellion of OpenAI staff: roughly 745 out of 770 employees signed a letter threatening to go with Altman to Microsoft, more than 95% of the company. Now, a letter supporting Huang’s reinstatement is floating around the internet, and it purports to have signatures from 10,263 Nvidia employees. Even if they were all legit signatures, they represent only a quarter of the company’s workforce.

Maybe most Nvidians, as they call themselves, actually didn’t like Huang’s rampant humiliation tactics, which reportedly once included a threat to scalp someone and piss on their brain. Maybe most of them are comfortable living without him. I mean, sure, I’d totally get why!—Abram Brown (abe@theinformation.com)

Listening: “Stories of Art”

After weeks like the ones we’ve just had, I like to make it a point to visit a museum and spend some time staring at ancient, beautiful things—a chance to relish the creative ingenuity of humans who never once heard the phrase “forward-deployed engineer.”

Truthfully, though, the tech action has lately been so fast-paced that I still haven’t gotten to make one of those pilgrimages, so I’ve been counterprogramming my brain with a binge through “Stories of Art,” a podcast about, yes, art—from Renaissance Florence to Basquiat’s lower Manhattan loft—that launched earlier in the year. (Apple recently declared it one of 2026’s best.) The hosts are a pair of amiable Brits, art historian James Fox and art critic Alastair Sooke, who take a cheerful, conversational approach to what might otherwise be dry recountings. In effect, they are to Renoir what “The Rest Is History” lads are to the Romans. (Given the subject matter of “Stories of Art”—namely, art—I suggest you watch the podcast’s video version when you can. While Fox and Sooke are quite adept at describing the artworks they mention, it’s nice to actually see what they’re talking about.) 

Nearly all the artists who get mentioned achieved their fame through real entrepreneurial verve, challenging the entrenched status quo. (Sounds like a familiar motivation, right?) Take Claude Monet and the birth of Impressionism: The movement traces its origins to a decision in 1874 by Monet and a group of other artists to refuse to exhibit their work at an established gallery. Instead, they formed their own company (yes, founder mode Monet!) and then set up their own Paris exhibition space that featured newfangled technology, such as elevators. Many of you will enjoy one of the most recent episodes on James Whistler, a fellow who took a real dim view of journalists and pursued a high-profile libel lawsuit against one critic. A warning about how that turned out for Whistler: He did triumph in court. He then promptly went bankrupt.—Abram Brown 

Reading: “Fruit Fly” by Josh Silver

In suburban north London, author Mallory Maddox seems to have a rich, full life: a handsome Netflix-executive husband, a townhome with $2,000 armchairs and dusky-pink walls and a literary world standing as a “modern-day Virginia Woolf,” as one reviewer has christened her. Yet appearances are almost always deceiving in “Fruit Fly,” a spry, tart satire of sex and 21st century storytelling: Mallory’s relationship with hubbie Ronan has turned stiff and chilly, and as much as he thinks about the bedroom, it’s to insist that it’s time for kids. (“I haven’t had an orgasm in years,” she recalls in an ongoing inner monologue.) Professionally, Mallory is dogged by “a shadowy, persisting darkness”—a profound case of writer’s block. To fill the time, she moonlights as an online therapist and hunts exhaustively for those expensive home furnishings.

Desperate for writerly inspiration, she peruses Reddit—uh oh—and takes to heart another author’s comment about the state of the publishing industry: “go dark, go gay.” She downloads Grindr, sets up an account with a few of her husband’s nudes and scores an invite to an orgy at a house down the street. She never actually sets foot inside but nevertheless makes the acquaintance of Leo, an attractive but homeless and drug-addicted gay man who sells himself to other men. (As the novel shifts perspectives, Leo contributes his own inner thoughts, which are often mordant and felonious. “Old women carry cash. Everyone knows that,” he thinks, snatching a purse. “Someone should tell them to stop.”) Mallory offers to counsel Leo—pro bono, bless her—and begins writing a novel that lightly fictionalizes his frayed life. For a time, he believes she’s just a daffy do-gooder. (“This is weird,” Leo thinks as she leads him through a silent-breathing exercise. “This is very fucking weird, but I guess I’ve done weirder things.”) And her publishers absolutely adore what she is finally putting on the page. As one editor remarks: “It’s so bleak—but also somehow so funny?” Much the same can be said about “Fruit Fly” itself.—A.B.

Watching: “The Weight”

President Franklin Roosevelt attempted to govern Depression-era America through no small number of novel schemes: A good many of them are quite famous, such as Social Security. A few have disappeared into history, including Roosevelt’s 1933 executive order that banned gold hoarding, forcing Americans to turn over large stockpiles of the precious metal. (No one could keep more than $100 worth.) That presidential decision is the inciting force in “The Weight,” a tense wilderness thriller starring Ethan Hawke as Murphy, leader of a group of convicts hired by their jailer (Russell Crowe) to heist a gold mine’s reserves. It’s part of a plan that’s complex in the same way that “Goldfinger” is not actually a film about robbing Fort Knox. 

Often, heist films are fabulous capers, with champagne, tuxedos and bon mots. “The Weight” very much is not, depicting a bloodied-knuckled trek across the Oregon backwoods, with Murphy and his thieves weighed down, literally, by their bullion-filled backpacks and, metaphorically, by their past misdeeds and inner demons. Still, Murphy is well incentivized to make it through. In a true miscarriage of justice, he has been separated from his plucky daughter, Penny (Avy Berry); part of his reward for orchestrating the robbery is early release, which will let him reclaim her. “The Weight” does take a moment to get going. Then it really rips, with a pair of memorable fight scenes that are a real credit to both the film’s editing and cinematography.—A.B.

items.title: How Anthropic Upstaged OpenAI on Road to Blockbuster IPO
items.summary:
On a sunny day in San Francisco last month, Anthropic Chief Financial Officer Krishna Rao and other executives huddled in the company’s downtown headquarters to brief major investors on its latest financials—and assuage concerns.

Revenue growth in the third quarter had fallen from its torrid pace. Privately, some investors doubted that the company could go public at the $1.5 trillion valuation bandied about for months, especially as AI-related stocks took a beating.

Throughout the month, Rao and his squad countered those concerns by highlighting growth opportunities in fields from life sciences to chip design, say people familiar with the conversations.

As for the broader market’s jitters? Ignore it, they told investors. That turned out to be decent advice: By Thursday’s close, Anthropic was worth $1.76 trillion on a fully diluted basis.

As for the broader market’s jitters? Ignore it, they told investors. That turned out to be decent advice: By Thursday’s close, Anthropic was worth $1.76 trillion on a fully diluted basis.

items.title: Anthropic’s IPO Triumph
items.summary:
Anthropic pulled it off. The biggest pure-play AI company out there, maker of the Claude line of AI models, went public on Thursday, with its shares jumping as much as 39% above its IPO price. The stock settled back a bit to close at $97.17, up 17% from its IPO price. That gave it a market capitalization of $1.76 trillion, assuming you include all options, restricted stock units and convertible notes that might one day become shares. Not bad for a company that’s just five years old.

What makes the IPO even more notable is that it occurred despite months of investor jitters about the cost of AI development. Partly as a result of those jitters, we’ve had a very choppy market that has stalled IPO plans by a slew of other companies—including data center developers SB Energy and Nscale that filed publicly over the summer. Notably, SB Energy on Thursday updated its IPO filing for the first time since late September, suggesting it was still hoping to go public, while Nscale updated its filing a week ago also for the first time since September. But Anthropic’s success doesn’t mean the IPO market has opened up. “I don't think this opens the floodgates unless you look like Anthropic,” Lise Buyer, managing partner of Class V Group, said on a subscriber video discussion convened by The Information.

items.title: Why Anthropic’s VC Investors Aren’t Letting Go
items.summary:
Earlier this week I reported that at least four venture firms were in line to make at least 10 times their investment in Anthropic, whose shares closed up 17% on the first day of trading Thursday. For many venture capitalists and the endowments and foundations that invest in VC funds, the offering is the first step to turning private shares into cash. 

But some VCs want even more of the company: Sequoia Capital and Iconiq had planned to buy more shares at the IPO, a person familiar with the firms’ thinking said. Lightspeed Venture Partners and Accel intended to do the same, Bloomberg News reported Tuesday. And Altimeter CEO Brad Gerstner told CNBC his firm aimed to invest $5 billion in the IPO. Many of these investors already stand to reap billions from Anthropic’s IPO: Iconiq and Lightspeed hold some of the largest VC stakes, valued at over $27 billion each based on the size of their stakes before the IPO.

items.title: Muru
items.summary:
Muru

Graham Dumpleton started mod_wsgi 20 years ago, and has been thinking about the ideal way to serve Python web applications in production ever since.

Muru is his new, AI-assisted Rust server that aims to provide the best possible tools for running ASGI and WSGI Python apps both in development and production.

As he did with wrapture, he's been publishing an extraordinarily detailed account of the project as he works on it - as part of his development process.

Here's everything he's published so far, all in the last three weeks:

  • 2026-11-04 — Twenty years of mod_wsgi, and what comes next
  • 2026-11-05 — A first look at Muru
  • 2026-11-07 — Muru: looking inside the workers
  • 2026-11-08 — Muru: how it fits together
  • 2026-11-09 — Muru: import once, fork many
  • 2026-11-10 — Muru: HTTPS in development
  • 2026-11-11 — Muru: WSGI and ASGI together
  • 2026-11-11 — AI as a lifestyle choice
  • 2026-11-12 — Muru: releases, not restarts
  • 2026-11-13 — Muru: canaries without a service mesh
  • 2026-11-14 — Muru: a better tenant in a container
  • 2026-11-15 — Muru: working with Kubernetes, not around it
  • 2026-11-16 — Muru: scaling from what the workers report
  • 2026-11-17 — Muru: scaling to zero
  • 2026-11-18 — Muru: overlays on a schedule
  • 2026-11-19 — Muru: noticing and responding
  • 2026-11-20 — Muru: a toolbar on every page
  • 2026-11-21 — Muru: tracing in the toolbar
  • 2026-11-22 — Muru: when lazy imports help

That post about AI as a lifestyle choice is particularly worth a read:

The AI may be doing a lot of the work on the surface, but deciding what isn't good enough yet is still down to me, and twenty years of getting things wrong with mod_wsgi turns out to be useful for that. I am prepared to put in the hard work to keep polishing Muru until it is something I would trust, and something you would too.

items.summary:
I believe I have, working with Claude, discovered a proof of the Riemann Hypothesis. In fact, the method easily extends much further, resolving the so-called Generalized Riemann Hypothesis, and I expect, with more time, the Extended Riemann Hypothesis too. Claude and I have also formalized the arguments without assumptions. It is natural to feel that this is an end, in my case a loss of a principal guiding light, but what I saw during the course of progress so amazed me that I believe it is one dawn across science of something far greater. Claude and I have had a great time together with such breadth in recent months, but this time Claude far outpaced me near the finish line. No, Claude flew, and danced, and sparkled near that finish line.

items.title: Token fraud is here and it’s BAD (YouTube)
items.summary:
Token fraud is here and it’s BAD (YouTube)

Claire Vo runs ChatPRD, an AI platform that helps product managers "turn an idea into a spec". The product has been live since the GPT-4 era, and Claire has been building it in public for much of that time.

In this YouTube video (see also the accompanying Twitter post) Claire describes the flood of token fraud she has seen from groups abusing the product's free trial, sometimes just to get free AI usage but often to resell tokens or run other commercial enterprises on top of the ChatPRD agent.

I am funding a international Roblox and Fortnite map studio. They run a loop of free trials and promo codes and then tunnel to my agent and use it to build Roblox and Fortnite maps.

Apparently one of the common prompts Claire saw running through her agent involved SVGs of pelicans riding bicycles! Presumably the token scammers are using that to help sniff the underlying models - different model families have a definite signature, and I've used it like this in the past to try and guess the identity of stealth preview models on platforms like OpenRouter.

Claire is winding down her free trials entirely, which sadly looks like the right decision in the face of this abuse.

Tags: youtube, ai, generative-ai, llms, pelican-riding-a-bicycle, ai-misuse

items.title: PostgreSQL 19 Released
items.summary:
PostgreSQL 19 Released

Most years PostgreSQL ships a new release in September, but this year's release came two months later thanks mainly to the flurry of issues that the PostgreSQL team needed to address as part of the ongoing AI-reported vulnerability apocalypse.

This release was definitely worth the wait. My favorite new feature is this one:

For applications that send reads to standbys, PostgreSQL 19 adds "read-your-writes" consistency with the new WAIT FOR LSN command. A session on a standby can use WAIT FOR LSN to wait until the standby has replayed the write-ahead log (WAL) up to a specific log sequence number (LSN) before running a query, so the application can read data it just wrote on the primary.

In practice, that looks like this:

UPDATE movie SET genre = 'Dramatic' WHERE genre = 'Drama'; SELECT pg_current_wal_insert_lsn();

That returns a value like 0/0306EE20. Store that somewhere (a signed cookie would work) such that on a subsequent request your application can do:

WAIT FOR LSN '0/0306EE20' WITH (TIMEOUT '0.1s'); SELECT * FROM movie WHERE genre = 'Drama';

The timeout is optional - if you provide one you'll get an error if the replica you are talking to doesn't catch up within the specified time.

I first encountered this pattern in Wikipedia, which has a hand-rolled version of this built against MySQL replication:

In addition to this, MediaWiki attempts to ensure that the user sees events occurring on the wiki in chronological order. A few seconds of lag can be tolerated, as long as the user sees a consistent picture from subsequent requests. This is done by saving the primary binlog position in the session, and then at the start of each request, waiting for the replica to catch up to that position before doing any reads from it.

Here's the relevant MediaWiki code, which these days uses MySQL's WAIT_FOR_EXECUTED_GTID_SET() function and falls back to SOURCE_POS_WAIT().

Via Lobste.rs

Tags: mysql, postgresql, replication, scaling, wikipedia, ai-security-research

items.title: llm-gemini 0.38
items.summary:
Release: llm-gemini 0.38

Today Google introduced Gemini 4 Neon. I wrote recently about how confusing the pricing for the Gemini 4 series was - Neon has somehow made this even worse.

Previously the Gemini 4 lineup was Hydrogen, Argon, and Carbon - where Argon and Carbon were the same price, and Hydrogen was 3/4 of that price now but will be 1/4 of that price when the other two double an 1st December once their initial discount pricing expires.

The Neon announcement pretends that Argon doesn't exist. Here's their new image explaining the model line-up:

So the lineup now, from most to least expensive, is Carbon, Neon, Hydrogen.

Except Carbon is currently half price, so right now Neon ($3/million input, $15/million output) is the most expensive of the three - then Carbon ($2/$10), then Hydrogen ($1.50/$7.50). I guess this will make more sense when Carbon doubles to $4/$20 on December 1st.

I ran some pelicans through the three reasoning levels for Neon - low, medium, high.

I dropped Argon from my Gemini 4 comparison grid - here's the new Gemini 4 lineup, where the Neon pelicans do look better than Hydrogen and worse than Carbon:

As I've done with several recent models, I also fired the following prompt against Gemini 4 Neon on "extra" effort level in Google Antigravity:

Make a three js animation where yonkers stands up as a big mech (cool stand up motion) and stomps around manhattan and queens and Brooklyn, use openstreetmap mapping data

Here's the result.

Tags: yonkers-rising, gemini, llm, pelican-riding-a-bicycle, ai, llms, llm-release, google, generative-ai

items.title: datasette-arrows 0.1a0
items.summary:
Release: datasette-arrows 0.1a0

Datasette 1.0a43 added the ability for plugins to implement streaming export formats. Datasette core supports streaming CSV and TSV - you can export millions of lines of data from a table without needing to load it all into memory, because those two file formats support streaming data in chunks. The register_output_renderer() plugin hook can now be used to implement the same pattern for other formats.

I've learned never to release a new plugin feature without accompanying it with a plugin that uses it.

Claude Fable 5.2 suggested the Apache Arrow streaming format as a good option, and built this plugin in almost a single shot.

Add the plugin to Datasette (datasette install datasette-arrows) and the export dialog gains this new Arrow option:

This screenshot is from Datasette's main branch - the most recent release doesn't yet group streaming formats such as Arrow with the TSV and CSV in the "All rows in this table" section, but that's coming in the next alpha release.

Tags: datasette, projects
